text: Standard Japanese, Osaka and Kyoto, and a tour of other regions.
Japan has lots of dialects, called 方言, hōgen. Standard Japanese is based on Tokyo speech; it's what TV, schools and this app use, and everyone understands it.
Kansai-ben is the big one: Osaka, Kyoto and Kobe. Its melody is different, and some word pairs even swap their pitch. Thank you can be おおきに.
Osaka-ben is lively and famous for comedy. ほんま means really, あかん means no good, and a comedian's comeback is なんでやねん!
Osaka: なんでやねん, roughly 'why on earth?!', the classic retort in manzai comedy.
Kansai says へん for 'not'. 行かない becomes 行かへん.
Kyoto-ben is soft and polite. It's famous for はる, a gentle way to show respect: 来はる, they come.
Kyoto's traditional welcome, heard at old shops and teahouses: おいでやす.
Fukuoka has Hakata-ben, famous for this sweet line: 好いとーよ, I like you.
Hiroshima says じゃけえ for 'so' or 'because'.
Nagoya says でら for 'very'. でらうまい is 'really tasty'.
In the north, Tōhoku, べ is common: 行くべ, let's go.
Okinawa has its own Ryukyuan languages. めんそーれ is the famous welcome.
My voice reads all of these with a standard melody, so listen to real locals for the true accent. And use standard Japanese anywhere: it always works!
Word order, the verb at the end, and leaving words out.
In Japanese the verb comes last. The basic order is: the topic, then the details, then the verb.
Little words called particles come after a word and give it its job. Here に marks where you're going.
If it's obvious who you mean, leave them out. Japanese drops 'I' and 'you' all the time.
Time and place go before the verb too. A common order is: topic, time, place, object, verb.
The verb's ending shows the tense: 食べます is eat, 食べました is ate. More on that in Verbs and tenses.
For 'X is Y', use X は Y です. です at the end is the polite 'is'.
The little words after each word that say what it's doing.
は marks the topic: what the sentence is about. It's written は but said 'wa'.
を marks the object, the thing you do something to. It's said 'o'.
に is a point: the time something happens, or where you're going.
で is where something happens, or how you do it, like by train.
へ means 'toward'. It's written へ but said 'e'. It's close to に for going places.
と means 'with', or 'and' between nouns.
も means 'too' or 'also'. It replaces は, が or を.
の links two nouns, like 'of' or an apostrophe-s: 私の名前 is 'my name'.
が points at the subject, and goes with likes and wants: 猫が好き, I like cats.
か at the end turns a polite sentence into a question.
Two tenses, polite and casual, and the three kinds of verbs.
Japanese has just two tenses: past, and not past. The same form covers now and the future.
Here the same 行きます means 'will go', because of 明日, tomorrow.
For the past, ます becomes ました.
For 'don't', ます becomes ません. The past negative is ませんでした.
Casual speech uses the plain form instead. Same meaning, for friends and family.
Verbs come in three kinds. ru-verbs drop る, u-verbs change their last sound, and two are irregular.
ています means doing right now, or a state that's ongoing.
To say you want to do something, add たいです to the verb stem.
です, the two kinds of adjectives, and their past and negative.
Nouns use です for 'is'. In casual speech it's だ, and often just dropped.
い-adjectives end in い. You can add です to be polite.
い-adjectives change their own ending: 高い, 高くない, 高かった. Don't say 高いでした.
な-adjectives work like nouns, with です and だ.
Before a noun, な-adjectives add な: 静かな町, a quiet town. い-adjectives don't: 高い山.
One exception: いい, good, becomes よ in its other forms: よくない, よかった.
か, what, where, when, who, and how to answer.
For a polite question, just add か to the end. No change in word order.
何 means what. Before です it's said なん.
どこ means where. You'll use this one a lot.
いつ means when.
誰 means who.
Casually, drop か and raise your voice, or end with の.
To answer, people usually repeat the verb: 行きます, or 行きません. はい means yes.
Please do, won't you, let's: the て-form and friends.
To ask someone to do something, use the て-form plus ください.
ru-verbs make the て-form by swapping る for て.
u-verbs change by their last sound. 行く is the one exception: 行って.
To invite, ask in the negative with ませんか: won't you?
ましょう means 'let's'.
With friends, the casual 'let's' ends in おう or よう.
Verb groups: dictionary form → polite form. Tap any form to hear it.
食べる, to eat. ru-verb: drop る and add the ending.
行く, to go. u-verb: the last sound changes (く → き, か, こ…).
する, to do. Irregular: just memorise it. It also makes many verbs: 勉強する (to study).
来る, to come. Irregular: the reading of 来 changes (く, こ, き).
て-form: dictionary form → て-form. Tap any form to hear it.
高い, expensive, tall. い-adjective: it changes its own ending.
静か, quiet. な-adjective: works like a noun with だ/です; add な before a noun (静かな町).
学生, student (a noun). Nouns use だ / です. Formal writing says ではありません for the negative.

Five lines, four spaces, and the notes that live on them. Tap any note on the staff to hear it.
Music is written on a staff: five lines and four spaces. The higher a note sits, the higher it sounds.
This curly sign is the treble clef. It wraps around the second line from the bottom, and that line is G.
The lines, bottom to top, are E, G, B, D, F. Remember them as Every Good Boy Does Fine.
The spaces spell a word: F, A, C, E. FACE!
Middle C sits on its own short line below the staff, called a ledger line. It's near the middle of a piano.
C to C, Japan's ドレミ, and sharps and flats. Tap any note on the staff to hear it.
Notes are named with seven letters: C D E F G A B, then it starts again at C, one octave higher.
In Japan, school music uses ドレミ: ド レ ミ ファ ソ ラ シ ド. Sing along!
Japanese key names use older kana: ハ ニ ホ ヘ ト イ ロ for C D E F G A B. So C major is ハ長調.
A sharp sign raises a note by a half step. Listen: F, then F sharp.
A flat lowers a note by a half step. On a piano, sharps and flats are mostly the black keys.
Whole, half, quarter and eighth notes, dots and rests. Tap any note on the staff to hear it.
A whole note is an open oval with no stem. It lasts four beats.
A half note is open with a stem: two beats each.
A quarter note is filled in with a stem: one beat each.
An eighth note has a little flag: half a beat, so two fit in one beat.
A dot adds half the note's length again. A dotted half lasts three beats.
Rests are silences with the same lengths. Here: note, rest, note, rest.
Bar lines, time signatures, and your first melody. Tap any note on the staff to hear it.
Bar lines split music into bars. The numbers at the start are the time signature: 4 over 4 means four quarter-note beats in every bar.
3 over 4 means three beats in a bar, like a waltz: ONE two three, ONE two three.
Let's read a real tune: the start of きらきら星, Japan's Twinkle Twinkle. Follow each note as I hum it.
Now the next line. Notice it steps down: F, E, D, C.

Eight easy chords get you through hundreds of songs. Each diagram shows the strings, low E on the left, and where to press. Tap a diagram to strum it.
C major: a bright, happy chord. Skip the low E string. Its shape is x 3 2 0 1 0.
G major: big and open. All six strings ring. Its shape is 3 2 0 0 0 3.
D major: just the top four strings, a little triangle shape. Its shape is x x 0 2 3 2.
E minor: only two fingers! Minor chords sound softer and sadder. Its shape is 0 2 2 0 0 0.
A minor: the same shape as E major, moved over one string. Its shape is x 0 2 2 1 0.
E major: like Em, plus one finger on the G string. Its shape is 0 2 2 1 0 0.
D minor: top four strings, a gentle, wistful sound. Sakura Sakura uses it. Its shape is x x 0 2 3 1.
F major 7: an easy stand-in for F, which needs a hard barre. It sounds dreamy. Its shape is x x 3 2 1 0.
Try switching between C, G, Am and Em: that's the chords of countless pop songs. Tap each to hear it.
Here's a chord library. Tap any diagram to hear it. Open chords first, then sevenths, barre chords and J-rock power chords.
Open chords. Tap each one to strum it.
Sevenths: the J-pop colour. Tap each one to strum it.
Barre chords. Tap each one to strum it.
Power chords: J-rock. Tap each one to strum it.
One finger across all six strings: the key to every chord up the neck. Tap any diagram to hear it.
A barre chord uses your first finger like a capo, pressing every string at one fret. The bar in the diagram shows it.
F is the famous first barre chord. Roll your first finger slightly onto its bony side, keep your thumb behind the neck, and press close to the fret wire.
Bm is a barre from the A string at the 2nd fret. Skip the low E string.
The magic: slide one barre shape up the neck and it becomes a new chord. The F shape at fret 3 is G; at fret 5 it's A.
It's normal for barres to buzz at first. A few minutes a day builds the strength. Until then, Fmaj7 is a friendly stand-in for F.
Two or three notes, loud and punchy: the sound of J-rock. Tap any diagram to hear it.
A power chord is just a root note and its fifth, often with the octave on top. It's written with a 5, like E5.
No third means it's neither major nor minor, so it stays clean even with heavy distortion. That's why rock bands love it.
The shape moves anywhere: root on the low E or A string, fifth two frets up on the next string.
Try E5, then G5, then A5. That shape slide is in countless rock riffs.
For the J-rock drive, play fast down-strums with your palm resting lightly on the strings near the bridge. That's palm muting.
Kick, snare and hi-hat, and how to count a beat.
The kick drum is the big low thump, played with your foot. It's the heartbeat of the song.
The snare is the sharp crack in the middle, usually on beats 2 and 4. That's the backbeat.
The hi-hat is the ticking cymbal that keeps time, usually on every eighth note.
Drummers count sixteenths as one-e-and-a, two-e-and-a, and so on. Each square in the grid is one of those.
Put it together and you get the 8-beat: the basic rock and J-pop groove. Next, play it yourself!
Four strings, root notes, and locking in with the kick.
The bass has four strings: E, A, D and G, an octave lower than a guitar's lowest four.
The bass player's first job is the root: the note the chord is named after. C chord, play C.
Lock in with the kick drum: when the kick hits, the bass usually plays too. Together they're the rhythm section.
Then add movement: the octave above the root, or the fifth. Same chord, more bounce.

Our eight planets, to scale, with a fact about each.
Here's the solar system in 3D! Drag to spin it, pinch to zoom, and tap a planet to hear its name. Sizes and distances are squeezed so everything fits.
Eight planets go around the Sun. Here they are at their real sizes compared with each other.
Mercury: The smallest planet and the closest to the Sun. A single day there, sunrise to sunrise, lasts longer than its year.
Venus: The hottest planet, about 465 °C, because its thick carbon dioxide air traps heat. It spins backwards compared with most planets.
Earth: The only planet known to have liquid water on its surface and life.
Mars: Red because of iron oxide (rust) in its dust. It has Olympus Mons, the tallest volcano known in the solar system.
Jupiter: The biggest planet: about eleven Earths would fit across it. Its Great Red Spot is a storm bigger than Earth.
Saturn: Famous for its rings of ice and rock. It's so light for its size that, on average, it's less dense than water.
Uranus: Tipped over by about 98 degrees, so it rolls around the Sun on its side.
Neptune: The farthest planet, with the fastest winds measured in the solar system, around 2,000 km/h.
In Japanese, five planets are named after the old elements: water, metal, fire, wood and earth. They also give us the days of the week!
Find Orion, the North Star and the Tanabata stars, from their real positions.
Orion the hunter rules winter evenings. The three stars in a row are his belt, called 三つ星 in Japanese. Red Betelgeuse was once called 平家星 and white Rigel 源氏星, after the two rival clans.
Betelgeuse, Sirius and Procyon make the Winter Triangle. Sirius is the brightest star in the whole night sky.
Follow the two stars at the end of the Big Dipper's bowl, Merak then Dubhe, about five times their distance apart, and you reach Polaris, the North Star.
Cassiopeia is a W (or M) shape on the opposite side of the North Star from the Big Dipper, so when one is low in the sky, the other is high.
Vega (織姫星), Altair (彦星) and Deneb make the Summer Triangle. In the Tanabata legend, the Milky Way flows between the two lovers, Vega and Altair. Deneb sits in the swan, Cygnus.
Now look around a real night sky in 3D: every bright star here is placed from its real position. Drag to look up, down and around, and tap a star to name it.
Constellations are patterns people imagine; the stars in them can be very different distances away. Light from Betelgeuse takes hundreds of years to reach us.
a² + b² = c²: the long side of any right triangle.
A right triangle has one square corner. The longest side, opposite that corner, is the hypotenuse, c.
Build a square on each side. Count them: 9 little squares plus 16 makes 25. The two small squares always add up to the big one.
Why? Fit four copies of the triangle inside a big square. The space left in the middle is exactly c squared. Rearrange them and it becomes a squared plus b squared.
Real life: a 5 metre ladder with its foot 3 metres from the wall reaches 4 metres up. And a TV's size is its diagonal: the hypotenuse!
In Japan it's called 三平方の定理, the three-squares theorem. Try your own numbers!
How saving and investing grow, and why starting early matters.
Simple interest pays only on what you put in. Compound interest also pays on the interest you've already earned, so growth earns growth.
The rule of 72: divide 72 by the yearly growth rate to find roughly how many years it takes to double. At 6%, about 12 years.
Small amounts add up. Try it: change the monthly amount, the growth rate and the years.
Investments go up and down, and returns are never guaranteed. Fees and inflation matter too. This is a lesson in the maths, not financial advice.
Why a little every day beats a lot once in a while.
Fifteen minutes a day is over 91 hours in a year: more than two working weeks of study, with no single long day.
Spacing works: memory fades quickly after we learn something, but each review slows the fading. Short daily sessions give you those reviews. Psychologists call it the spacing effect.
Small gains compound too: getting 1% better each day multiplies to about 37 times over a year, because 1.01 to the power 365 is 37.8. It's a nice piece of maths, not a promise!
Make it easy: same time each day, a tiny goal, and stop while it's still fun. That's why Aoi's lessons are short!
Where your heart is, its four chambers, and how blood flows, with real anatomy plates.
Meet your heart! This is a friendly cartoon model. Drag to turn it all the way round, and tap each part to hear its name.
Your heart sits in the middle of your chest, behind the breastbone, between your two lungs, tipped a little to the left. It's about the size of your fist.
The lungs wrap around it on both sides. In body pictures you're facing the person, so their left side is on your right.
It has four rooms: two atria on top that collect blood, and two ventricles below that pump it out. Tap them on the model! Blue is the right side, red is the left.
The right side sends blood to the lungs to pick up oxygen; the left side pumps it to the whole body.
The two big tubes on top are the aorta, carrying blood to the body, and the pulmonary artery, carrying it to the lungs. The heart even feeds itself through little coronary arteries on its surface.
An adult's resting heart usually beats about 60 to 100 times a minute: around 100,000 times a day. Feel your pulse at your wrist or neck!
Recording a mic or a guitar into FL Studio, step by step.
You need an audio interface: it has a mic input with a preamp, an instrument input for guitar or bass, and headphone and speaker outputs.
In Options, Audio settings, choose your interface's ASIO driver on Windows, or its device on a Mac. While recording, a small buffer, like 128 or 256 samples, keeps the delay low.
Open the Mixer and pick an empty insert track. In the insert's input menu, choose your interface's input: input 1 for a mic, for example.
Arm the insert for recording with its record button, and set your level so the loudest bits peak around minus 12 to minus 6 dB. Never let it hit red.
Press the record button, choose recording audio into the Playlist as an audio clip, turn on the metronome and a count-in, then press play and perform.
Tips: record without heavy effects (you can add them later), use a pop filter for vocals, and plug guitar into the instrument input, adding an amp-sim plugin afterwards.
Balancing your tracks so everything can be heard.
Send every instrument to its own mixer insert, so each one gets its own volume, panning and effects.
Start with levels and panning: get a rough balance with the faders before any plugins. Leave headroom on the master.
EQ: with Fruity Parametric EQ 2, cut low rumble below about 80 to 100 Hz on things that aren't bass or kick, and cut clashing frequencies before boosting.
Compression evens out loud and soft moments, so a vocal sits steadily in the mix. Use gentle settings at first.
Put reverb and delay on send tracks, and send a little of each instrument to them. That glues everything into one space.
Check your mix quietly, on headphones and on a phone speaker, compare it with a song you like, and take breaks: ears get tired.
The final polish before you share your song.
Mastering is the last step: gentle EQ and compression on the whole mix, then a limiter at the very end of the master chain.
The limiter, like Fruity Limiter, stops peaks going over a ceiling. Set the ceiling around minus 1 dB so the file doesn't distort after streaming conversion.
Streaming services turn loud songs down to about the same loudness, often around minus 14 LUFS, so squashing your song super loud doesn't win. A loudness meter helps.
Export a WAV at 24-bit for the master; make MP3s from that. Listen on several speakers before you release.
What each kind of pedal does, the usual order, and a board you can hear.
Pedals change your guitar's sound before it reaches the amp. Switch some on and strum!
Drive pedals add grit: overdrive is warm and light, distortion is heavy, fuzz is wild and woolly. Turn on Distortion and play the riff.
Modulation pedals move the sound: chorus shimmers, tremolo pulses the volume, and phasers and flangers swoosh.
Time pedals add space: delay repeats what you play, reverb puts you in a room or hall.
A common order: tuner, wah, compressor, drive, modulation, delay, then reverb. Rules can be broken, but that's a great start.
Fire-breathing Western dragons and rain-bringing Eastern ones, and why dragons rule isekai.
Dragons appear in stories all over the world, but East and West imagined them very differently.
The Western dragon is a huge winged reptile that often breathes fire and guards treasure. In old European stories, like Saint George's, it's a monster for a hero to defeat.
The Eastern dragon, from China, is long like a snake and has no wings, yet it flies through the clouds. It brings rain and good luck, and it was a symbol of the emperor.
In Japanese the dragon is 龍 or 竜, read ryū or tatsu. Ryūjin, 龍神, is the dragon god of the sea, and in the tale of Urashima Tarō his undersea palace is Ryūgū-jō.
Count the claws! Chinese imperial dragons were usually drawn with five, and Japanese dragons often with three.
The dragon, 辰 tatsu, is one of the twelve zodiac animals. 2024 was a dragon year, and the next one is 2036.
In isekai and fantasy anime, dragons are often the strongest creatures of all: a final boss, a wise ancient guardian, or a surprisingly friendly ally.
Foxes, tanuki, kappa, tengu and oni: Japan's folklore creatures, with real Edo-period drawings.
Yokai, 妖怪, are the spirits and creatures of Japanese folklore. Some are spooky, some are silly, and some are kind.
Kitsune, the fox. Foxes are messengers of Inari, the god of rice, so Inari shrines have fox statues. Old stories say a fox grows more tails as it gets older and wiser, up to nine.

Tanuki, the raccoon dog, is a real animal in Japan! In stories it's a jolly shape-shifter that puts a leaf on its head to transform. Tanuki statues in big straw hats welcome guests outside restaurants. The emoji is a raccoon, its lookalike.
Kappa live in rivers. A kappa has a dish of water on its head, and if the water spills, it loses its strength! Kappa love cucumbers, which is why cucumber sushi rolls are called kappa-maki.
Tengu are mountain spirits with red faces and long noses, or crow beaks. They're masters of martial arts and fly with feathered fans.
Oni are ogres with horns, tiger-skin pants and iron clubs. On Setsubun, around February 3rd, families throw roasted soybeans and shout 鬼は外、福は内: demons out, good luck in!
A cat that lives for a very long time may become a nekomata, with its tail split in two. And rokurokubi look like ordinary people, until their necks stretch at night!

Old picture scrolls show the Hyakki Yagyō, the night parade of a hundred demons. In the 1700s the artist Toriyama Sekien drew hundreds of yokai in picture books, and his drawings still shape how yokai look in manga and anime today.
Slimes, elves, dwarves, goblins, fairies, mermaids, griffins and phoenixes, and where they really come from.
Isekai, 異世界, means another world. In isekai stories, the hero is transported or reborn into a fantasy world full of creatures like these.
The slime. In Western tabletop games slimes were dangerous oozes, but Japanese RPGs in the 1980s turned the slime into a cute, smiling beginner enemy. Now slimes are a symbol of isekai.
Elves come from Norse and Germanic folklore. Modern fantasy, starting with Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings, made them tall, graceful, long-lived archers with pointed ears.
Dwarves are also from Norse myth, where they forged the gods' treasures, like Thor's hammer, Mjölnir. In fantasy they're short, bearded miners and smiths.
Goblins are small, mischievous creatures from European folklore, and orcs were made famous by Tolkien. In isekai, goblins are often the first real fight for a new adventurer.

Fairies, yōsei, are small winged nature spirits. Mermaids, ningyo, are half human and half fish. Japan has its own mermaid legend: a girl who ate ningyo flesh lived for 800 years, the tale of Yao Bikuni.

Mix-and-match creatures! A griffin has an eagle's head and wings on a lion's body. A unicorn is a horse with one spiral horn. And the phoenix bursts into flame and is reborn from its ashes, which is why Japanese calls it 不死鳥, the bird that never dies.
Isekai stories borrow from video games too: a Demon Lord, 魔王 maō, rules the monsters, adventurers join a guild, and a status screen shows their level and skills, just like an RPG.
Brooms and cauldrons, Halloween, Baba Yaga, Merlin, Japan's onmyōji, and magical girls.
Witches, majo 魔女, and wizards, mahōtsukai 魔法使い, appear in stories all over the world.
In European folklore, witches brew potions in cauldrons, keep black cats, and fly on broomsticks.

Halloween, on October 31st, comes from Samhain, an old Celtic festival marking the end of the harvest, when spirits were believed to come close. Witches became a favourite Halloween costume, and Japan dresses up for it too.
Russia has Baba Yaga, a witch whose hut walks around on chicken legs! And Merlin is the famous wizard of the King Arthur legends, adviser to the king.
Japan's own wizard was the onmyōji, a court diviner who read the stars and calendars. Abe no Seimei, who lived about a thousand years ago, became a legend who could command spirits called shikigami.
Shrine maidens, miko 巫女, serve at Shinto shrines today, helping with ceremonies and sacred dances. In anime they often fight spirits with paper charms called ofuda.
Witch anime is a genre of its own: magical girls, mahō shōjo 魔法少女, transform with a wand or a charm and save the day. The genre began in Japan in the 1960s and is still going strong.
Shōnen, shōjo, isekai, mecha, slice of life and more: how anime genres work.
Anime has many genres, and Japan also sorts series by who they were first made for, based on the manga magazines they ran in.
Shōnen, 少年, means boy: action, friendship, training and rivals. Shōjo, 少女, means girl: feelings, romance and friendship. Anyone can enjoy either!
Seinen, 青年, is aimed at adult men and josei, 女性, at adult women: often more grown-up stories about work, life and love.
Isekai, 異世界: someone is transported or reborn into another world. Many began as web novels and light novels, and the genre boomed in the 2010s.
Magical girls, mahō shōjo 魔法少女, transform to fight evil. Mecha, メカ, are giant robots piloted from inside.
Slice of life, nichijō-kei 日常系, follows everyday school or work life. Iyashikei, 癒し系, healing anime, is calm and cosy, made to help you relax.
There's much more: sports, idols, romantic comedy, horror and sci-fi. Tap the heart on lessons you like, and switch on More please to ask for more of them!
Setsubun oni, Cat Day, Dog Day, carp that become dragons, Obon and Halloween in Japan.
Japan's calendar is full of days for creatures, real and imaginary. Here are the fun ones.
Setsubun, around February 3rd, marks the start of spring in the old calendar. Someone wears an oni mask, and everyone throws roasted soybeans and shouts 鬼は外、福は内!
February 22nd is Cat Day, 猫の日, because 2/22 can be read ニャンニャンニャン, nyan nyan nyan! And November 1st is Dog Day, 犬の日, because 11/1 is ワンワンワン, wan wan wan.
On Children's Day, May 5th, families fly carp streamers, koinobori. A legend says a carp that swims up a waterfall called the Dragon Gate becomes a dragon, so 登竜門 means a gateway to success.
At Obon in summer, families welcome their ancestors' spirits home. Some make little animals from vegetables: a cucumber horse so the spirits arrive fast, and an eggplant cow so they leave slowly.
Fushimi Inari Taisha in Kyoto, the head Inari shrine, has thousands of red torii gates and many fox statues, often holding a key or a jewel in their mouths.
And on October 31st, Japan's cities fill with Halloween costumes too: witches, yokai and anime characters side by side.
Triassic to Cretaceous, T. rex and Stegosaurus, why birds are dinosaurs, and Japan's own dinosaurs.
Dinosaurs ruled the land for about 165 million years. In Japanese they're 恐竜, kyōryū, terrible dragons, and the English name means terrible lizard.
The Age of Dinosaurs, the Mesozoic Era, has three periods: the Triassic, about 252 to 201 million years ago, the Jurassic, 201 to 145, and the Cretaceous, 145 to 66.
Tyrannosaurus rex lived right at the end, about 68 to 66 million years ago. It was around 12 metres long, with teeth as big as bananas.
Sauropods, like Brachiosaurus, were plant-eaters with very long necks. Some, like Argentinosaurus, may have been over 30 metres long: the biggest land animals ever.

Stegosaurus, with plates on its back and spikes on its tail, lived in the Jurassic. It died out about 80 million years before T. rex appeared, so we live closer in time to T. rex than T. rex did to Stegosaurus!

Flying pterosaurs and the sea's plesiosaurs were not dinosaurs, just their reptile cousins. But birds are dinosaurs! They evolved from small feathered dinosaurs, so a chicken is a living relative of T. rex.
About 66 million years ago, an asteroid around 10 kilometres wide hit Chicxulub, in what is now Mexico. Together with huge volcanic eruptions, it ended the age of the non-bird dinosaurs.
Japan has dinosaurs too! Fukui Prefecture has many finds, like Fukuiraptor, and a big dinosaur museum. Kamuysaurus, named after the Ainu word for a god, was found at Mukawa in Hokkaido.
Japan's six native breeds, Hachikō, the most popular pet dogs, and Dog Day.
Dog is 犬, inu, and Japanese dogs say ワンワン, wan wan. Japan has six native breeds, called 日本犬, nihon-ken.
All six, Akita, Kai, Kishu, Shiba, Shikoku and Hokkaido, are protected as Natural Monuments, 天然記念物.
The Shiba Inu, 柴犬, is the smallest: a foxy face, a curled tail, and a famously loud Shiba scream when it's unhappy.
The Akita, 秋田犬, is the biggest. Hachikō, an Akita, waited at Shibuya Station for his owner every day for almost ten years after his owner died. His statue there is a famous meeting place.
The Kai Ken, 甲斐犬, from Yamanashi, has a tiger-striped brindle coat. The Kishu is usually white, the Shikoku looks like a little wolf, and the tough Hokkaido Ken was bred for snowy Hokkaido.
Japan's most popular pet breeds are mostly small: the Toy Poodle, the Chihuahua, the Miniature Dachshund and the Pomeranian, with the Shiba close behind.
November 1st is Dog Day in Japan, 犬の日, because 11/1 sounds like ワンワンワン. Give your dog an extra walk!
Japanese Bobtails, calico cats, maneki-neko, a cat station master, cat islands and Cat Day.
Cat is 猫, neko, and cats say ニャー, nyā. Japan loves cats!
The Japanese Bobtail has a short, fluffy pom-pom tail from a natural gene, and it has lived in Japan for centuries.

A calico, 三毛猫 mikeneko, three-fur cat, is white, orange and black. Almost every calico is female: the orange and black colours come from the X chromosome, so a cat needs two Xs to show both. Male calicos are very rare.
The beckoning cat, 招き猫 maneki-neko, waves customers into shops. Many say a raised left paw invites customers and a raised right paw invites money and luck.
In 2007, a calico called Tama became station master of Kishi Station in Wakayama, and the tourists she drew helped save the little railway line.
Japan has cat islands, like Tashirojima and Aoshima, where the cats outnumber the people.

Popular breeds in Japan include the Scottish Fold and the Munchkin. The Fold's ears come from a cartilage gene that can cause painful joint problems, so many vets urge caution about breeding them. Plenty of Japan's cats are happy mixed breeds, 雑種.
February 22nd is Cat Day, 猫の日, because 2/22 sounds like ニャンニャンニャン!
Thousands of small cores working at once: graphics, shaders, VRAM, and why AI runs on GPUs.
A GPU, graphics processing unit, is a chip built to do thousands of small calculations at the same time.

A CPU has a few powerful cores that are great at doing different jobs one after another. A GPU has thousands of simpler cores that all do the same kind of job at once. That's called parallel processing.
A Full HD screen is 1920 by 1080 pixels: over 2 million. The GPU works out the colour of every one of them 60 or more times every second.

The graphics pipeline: 3D models are made of triangles. A vertex shader moves and turns the triangles, rasterizing turns them into pixels, and a pixel shader colours each pixel with light and textures.
GPUs have their own fast memory, VRAM, so textures and models sit right next to the cores that need them.

AI runs on GPUs because neural networks are mostly giant matrix multiplications: the same multiply and add, millions of times over. Modern GPUs even have special matrix units, like NVIDIA's Tensor Cores, just for this.

Programmers talk to GPUs through APIs: Vulkan, DirectX and Apple's Metal for graphics, and CUDA, NVIDIA's platform, for general computing. And the 3D planets and heart in this app are drawn by your phone's GPU, through WebGL!
A whole computer on one chip: big and little CPU cores, GPU, NPU, camera ISP, modem, and why phones get hot.
A phone chip is a system on a chip, an SoC: a whole computer squeezed onto one piece of silicon about the size of a fingernail.
Its CPU has two kinds of cores: big fast ones for heavy work, and small efficient ones that handle light jobs and save battery. Arm calls this idea big.LITTLE.
There's a GPU for graphics, an NPU or neural engine for AI features like face unlock and photo tricks, and an ISP, image signal processor, that turns the camera sensor's data into photos.
The modem connects to mobile networks like 4G and 5G, with radios for Wi-Fi and Bluetooth too, though some phones use a separate modem chip.
Most phone chips use the Arm instruction set: Apple's A-series, Qualcomm's Snapdragon, Google's Tensor and MediaTek's Dimensity are all Arm-based.
Transistors are tiny on and off switches, and a flagship phone chip has well over 10 billion of them. Names like 3 nanometre are labels for a manufacturing generation, not an exact measurement.
Heat is the enemy. Phones have no fans, so when the chip gets too hot it slows itself down to stay safe. That's called thermal throttling.
Code, editors, compilers, Git, debuggers, SDKs, AI helpers like Claude Code, and how chips are designed.
Software starts as source code: text written in a programming language like Python, JavaScript, Swift or C.
Developers write code in an editor or an IDE, an integrated development environment, like VS Code, Android Studio or Xcode. It highlights mistakes and helps you type.
A compiler translates code into the machine instructions a chip can run. Some languages, like Python, use an interpreter, which runs the code step by step instead.
Git keeps every version of your code, so you can undo mistakes and work with a team. GitHub hosts Git projects online. This app lives in one!
A debugger lets you pause a program and look inside it, line by line. Tests are small programs that check your program still works after every change.
SDKs, software development kits, give you ready-made tools for a platform, like the Android SDK for Android apps. Package managers like npm and pip fetch libraries other people wrote.
AI coding assistants like Claude Code can read a whole project, write code, run the tests and explain errors. This app was built that way!

Chips are coded too! Engineers describe circuits in hardware description languages like Verilog or VHDL, test them in simulators, try them on FPGAs, which are chips you can rewire with code, then send the design to a factory, called a foundry.
Tap the switches: logic gates, then a half adder, then a 4-bit adder, the heart of a CPU.
Every chip is built from logic gates: tiny circuits that take 1s and 0s in and give 1s and 0s out. Tap A and B and watch the gates change!
AND gives 1 only if both inputs are 1. OR gives 1 if either is. NOT flips a bit, and XOR gives 1 when the inputs are different. Here's every case in a truth table.
Gates are made of transistors acting as switches. A CMOS NAND gate needs just four transistors, and any circuit at all can be built from NAND gates alone.
Let's build a half adder, which adds two bits. The sum is A XOR B, and the carry is A AND B. Try 1 plus 1: sum 0, carry 1, which is 10, two in binary!
A full adder also takes a carry in, so adders can be chained. Four full adders make a 4-bit adder that adds numbers up to 15 plus 15. Tap the bits!
This is the heart of a CPU's ALU, the arithmetic logic unit. Real chips repeat blocks like this billions of times.

Want to make a real one? Beginners can design chips in Verilog, test them on an FPGA board, and even join open projects like Tiny Tapeout, which puts many small designs from different people onto one real chip.
The box step in 3/4 time: one-two-three, one-two-three.
A waltz is in 3/4 time: count ONE two three, ONE two three, with a slight lean on ONE.
Count 1: step forward with your left foot.
Count 2: step to the side and a little forward with your right foot.
Count 3: bring your left foot to close beside your right. That's half a box!
Count 1 again: step back with your right foot. Count 2: left foot to the side. Count 3: right foot closes. You've drawn a box on the floor!
Press play and step along: the box loops round. Stay tall, frame your arms, and rise slightly on counts 2 and 3. Your partner mirrors you: right foot back first.
Every box on a cheque, and how to keep it safe.
Here's a sample cheque, US style. Each part matters. Let's go through them.
Write today's date at the top right.
After 'Pay to the order of', write exactly who gets the money: a person's or a company's name.
In the box, write the amount in numbers, starting right next to the dollar sign so nothing can be squeezed in.
On the long line, write the amount in words, with cents as a fraction over 100, then draw a line to fill the space. The words are the legal amount if they don't match.
The memo line is optional: a note to yourself, like an invoice number. Then sign it the way your bank knows.
The numbers at the bottom are the bank's routing number, your account number, and the cheque number. Never sign a blank cheque, always use a pen, and write VOID across mistakes.
In Japan, personal cheques are rare; people use bank transfers, called 振込 (furikomi), and cheques, 小切手 (kogitte), are mostly for businesses.
How much to move, a safe warm-up, and a 6-round timer to do it with Aoi.
The World Health Organization suggests adults get 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity a week, like brisk walking, plus muscle-strengthening on at least 2 days. Children: about an hour a day.
Warm up for 5 to 10 minutes first: march, swing your arms, and roll your shoulders, so your muscles are ready.
Good form beats speed: in a squat, knees follow your toes and your back stays long; in a push-up, keep a straight line from head to heels. Wall or knee push-ups are a great start.
Stop if you feel chest pain, dizziness or sharp pain, and talk to a doctor before starting if you have a health condition.
Ready? Six moves, 30 seconds each, 15 seconds rest. I'll count you through!
Mint, ginger, chamomile, Japanese herbs and Kampo, and the golden safety rules. Knowledge, not medical advice.
Herbs, ハーブ, and medicinal plants, 薬草 yakusō, have been used for flavour and healing for thousands of years. This lesson is knowledge, not medical advice.
Peppermint tea is a classic after-dinner drink, and its menthol gives that cool feeling. Peppermint oil capsules have some research support for easing irritable bowel symptoms.
Ginger, shōga 生姜, has good evidence for easing nausea, including morning sickness, though pregnant people should check with their doctor. In Japan, pickled ginger, gari, comes with sushi.
Chamomile tea is a gentle, caffeine-free bedtime drink. It's in the daisy family, so people allergic to ragweed may react to it.
Japanese kitchens have their own herbs: shiso 紫蘇, mitsuba 三つ葉, myōga 茗荷 and yuzu peel. Green shiso leaves garnish sashimi.
Kampo, 漢方, is Japan's traditional herbal medicine, adapted from Chinese medicine. In Japan, doctors can prescribe about 148 Kampo formulas through national health insurance.

Natural doesn't mean safe! St John's wort can stop some medicines working, including birth control pills and some heart drugs. Foxglove is beautiful but poisonous; it gave us the heart medicine digoxin, used at an exact dose.

Golden rules: buy from reliable shops, never eat a wild plant you can't identify for certain, and tell your doctor or pharmacist about any herbs or supplements you take, especially if you're pregnant or on medicine.

Meet your customer. Maria runs a small hardware store and has used a paper ledger for 15 years. She isn't against technology on principle, but she's watched other ‘time-saving’ tools eat up more time than they saved.
Going in, Maria doubts the real ROI, and is worried about the learning curve for herself and her two employees. That's the real objection — your job is to answer it, not talk past it.
Lead with what actually breaks today, not a feature list — ask what goes wrong with the paper system before pitching anything.
Offer a real way to test it risk-free — a trial on a slow week, not a vague promise.
Address the learning curve directly instead of brushing past it; show how little setup actually takes rather than just claiming it's easy.
Meet your customer. David is an office manager at a mid-size accounting firm, eight months into a two-year contract with a competitor. He isn't thrilled with it, but switching feels like a hassle.
Going in, David feels stuck, worried about cancellation fees and migration downtime. That's the real objection — your job is to answer it, not talk past it.
Ask what specifically annoys him about the current service — that's the real lever, not a generic pitch.
Address switching costs head-on: can the cancellation fee be offset, or can a price be locked in now for when his contract ends?
Reduce the perceived risk by describing exactly how migration works and how little downtime to actually expect.
Meet your customer. Tom has had the same corded vacuum for twelve years. It's heavy and the cord is annoying, but it still picks things up.
Going in, Tom doesn't see the problem as worth solving, and is price-sensitive. That's the real objection — your job is to answer it, not talk past it.
Don't argue his vacuum is bad — ask about the specific moments it's annoying (cord length, carrying it upstairs) and let him surface the pain himself.
A live demo of weight and maneuverability beats describing specs on paper.
If price comes up, compare the cost against his actual usage, not a generic ‘it pays for itself’ line.
Meet your customer. Priya liked the product in the demo but says budget approval is frozen until next quarter.
Going in, Priya is genuinely budget-constrained, not necessarily uninterested. That's the real objection — your job is to answer it, not talk past it.
Ask if there's a smaller starting tier, or a pilot, that fits an existing smaller budget line.
Find out exactly when budget reopens and offer to lock in today's pricing for a later start date.
Don't push past a real financial constraint — respect it, and offer a concrete next step instead of pressure.
Meet your customer. Jordan likes the educational content but is worried about data privacy and screen time for their 8-year-old.
Going in, Jordan needs trust built before price even comes up. That's the real objection — your job is to answer it, not talk past it.
Lead with concrete privacy and safety details — what data is collected, what parental controls exist — before talking price or features.
Offer a time-limited or screen-time-capped trial so the concern is addressed structurally, not just reassured away verbally.
Let them ask questions and sit with the trust-building stage — don't rush past it to close.
Meet your customer. Alan mows and treats his own lawn every weekend. It takes him three-plus hours and the results are mediocre, but he takes some pride in doing it himself.
Going in, Alan has an identity attachment to DIY, not a purely economic objection. That's the real objection — your job is to answer it, not talk past it.
Respect the effort explicitly before pitching anything — don't make him feel judged for his current results.
Frame the service as freeing up his weekend for something he'd rather do, not as ‘you're bad at this.’
A one-time trial treatment, not a long contract, lowers the identity threat of switching.
Meet your customer. Keisha has basic employer-provided life insurance and assumes that's sufficient. She hasn't really thought about the gap.
Going in, Keisha is underinformed about her actual coverage, not resistant as such. That's the real objection — your job is to answer it, not talk past it.
Ask what her employer coverage actually covers — many people overestimate it — rather than just asserting it isn't enough.
Use her own numbers (income, dependents) to show any real gap, not generic industry statistics.
Avoid fear-based pressure — present the gap as information she can decide what to do with.
Meet your customer. Robert is 72, independent, and feels that a ‘medical alert button’ makes him seem old and dependent.
Going in, Robert resists for emotional, identity reasons, not price or features. That's the real objection — your job is to answer it, not talk past it.
The real objection here is emotional, not logical — address identity before features.
Reframe it as staying independent longer, not as fragility.
If a family member is part of the conversation, let their perspective support rather than lead — Robert needs to feel it's his choice.
Meet your customer. Yuki has already gotten three quotes and is explicitly trying to negotiate your price down to match the cheapest one.
Going in, Yuki wants the lowest price, and needs to understand what's actually different between quotes. That's the real objection — your job is to answer it, not talk past it.
Don't just drop the price — explain the specific differences in materials, craftsmanship, and warranty versus the cheap quote.
If there's room to negotiate, trade concessions (a longer lead time, a different wood) rather than simply caving on price.
It's fine to lose a price-only customer when the gap genuinely reflects a real quality difference — don't undercut your own value.

Regulations. Here are the key points. Tap Next any time to skip ahead.
An applicant must be at least 17 years old for airplane, rotorcraft, powered-lift, or weight-shift-control aircraft privileges (16 for glider or balloon).
For a pilot under 40, a third-class medical certificate is valid for 60 calendar months from the month of the exam; it is 24 months for a pilot who is 40 or older.

14 CFR 61.57 requires at least three takeoffs and three landings within the preceding 90 days, in an aircraft of the same category and class (and type, if a type rating is required), to carry passengers. In a tailwheel airplane the landings must be to a full stop.

BasicMed requires completing an approved online medical education course every 24 calendar months, plus a physical exam with a state-licensed physician every 48 months, using the FAA's comprehensive medical examination checklist.
14 CFR 61.57 requires the night takeoffs and landings to a full stop to be in an aircraft of the same category and class (and type, if required) as the one to be flown.
A flight review of at least 1 hour of flight training and 1 hour of ground training is required every 24 calendar months, with a logbook endorsement.
14 CFR 91.207 requires ELT battery replacement after 1 cumulative hour of use, or when 50 percent of its useful life (or charge) has expired, whichever comes first.
14 CFR 91.151 requires a day VFR fuel reserve of at least 30 minutes beyond the point of intended landing.
At night, 14 CFR 91.151 requires a fuel reserve of at least 45 minutes at normal cruising speed.
14 CFR 91.3 states the pilot in command is directly responsible for, and is the final authority as to, the operation of the aircraft.
14 CFR 61.113 allows a private pilot to share operating expenses with passengers as long as the pilot pays at least a pro rata share of those expenses.

Private pilots are generally prohibited from carrying passengers or property for compensation or hire. 14 CFR 61.113 lists narrow exceptions, such as pro rata expense sharing, flights incidental to a business, and certain charitable and search-and-location flights.
AROW is a common memory aid for the required aircraft documents: Airworthiness certificate, Registration, Operating limitations (including the POH/AFM), and Weight and balance data.
Airworthiness Directives are mandatory corrective actions issued by the FAA for safety-of-flight issues, and must be complied with as specified.
14 CFR 91.409 requires most aircraft to have an annual inspection within the preceding 12 calendar months to remain airworthy.
Aircraft used to carry persons for hire generally require a 100-hour inspection in addition to the annual, per 14 CFR 91.409.
For VFR flight above 3,000 feet AGL, magnetic courses 0 through 179 use odd thousands plus 500 feet, such as 5,500 or 7,500; courses 180 through 359 use even thousands plus 500 feet.
14 CFR 91.113 gives an aircraft in distress the right of way over all other air traffic.
Over congested areas, the minimum safe altitude is 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle within a 2,000-foot horizontal radius of the aircraft.

Over other than congested areas, the minimum safe altitude is 500 feet above the surface, except over open water or sparsely populated areas, where the aircraft may not be closer than 500 feet to any person, vessel, vehicle, or structure.

14 CFR 91.211 requires the required minimum flight crew to use supplemental oxygen for that part of the flight at cabin pressure altitudes above 12,500 feet MSL up through 14,000 feet MSL that is of more than 30 minutes duration.
Above 14,000 feet MSL cabin pressure altitude, the required minimum flight crew must use supplemental oxygen for the entire time at that altitude.

For every flight, 91.103 requires runway lengths at airports of intended use and takeoff and landing distance data. For a flight under IFR or not in the vicinity of an airport, it also requires weather reports and forecasts, fuel requirements, alternatives available if the flight cannot be completed as planned, and any known traffic delays.
14 CFR 91.15 permits dropping objects as long as reasonable precautions are taken to avoid injury or damage to persons or property on the surface.

BasicMed operations are limited to altitudes at or below 18,000 feet MSL and indicated airspeeds of 250 knots or less, along with other limits, including that the flight may not be for compensation or hire.
14 CFR 91.13 broadly prohibits careless or reckless operation of an aircraft that endangers the life or property of another.

Logbook entries document the date, aircraft make, model and identification, route of flight, and flight time, broken out by relevant categories such as day, night, actual or simulated instrument, and other conditions of flight.

14 CFR 61.31 requires a logbook endorsement from an authorized instructor after receiving the required ground and flight training for complex, high-performance, tailwheel, pressurized, and certain other aircraft.

A VFR flight plan is not legally required for most flights, but it is strongly recommended as a safety practice since it helps trigger search-and-rescue efforts if a flight becomes overdue; some airspace, such as an Air Defense Identification Zone, has its own flight plan requirements.
Maintenance records must be retained until the work is superseded or for minimum periods set by 14 CFR 91.417, documenting the aircraft's inspection and maintenance history.
14 CFR 91.207 lists specific exceptions to the ELT requirement, including certain flight training operations conducted within 50 nautical miles of the airport from which the flight originated.
Transponder tests and inspections under 14 CFR 91.413 must have been performed within the preceding 24 calendar months for the transponder to be used to satisfy ATC requirements.
Airspace. Here are the key points. Tap Next any time to skip ahead.
Class A airspace extends from 18,000 feet MSL up to and including FL600 (60,000 feet).
Class B airspace requires an explicit ATC clearance to enter, not merely two-way radio contact.
Class C requires establishing, and maintaining, two-way radio communication with the controlling ATC facility before entry; a specific clearance is not required, only radio contact.
Like Class C, Class D requires two-way radio communication to be established with ATC before entering the airspace.
Much of the Class E airspace over the United States begins at 1,200 feet AGL; some begins at 700 feet AGL near certain airports, and some extends to the surface.
Class G is uncontrolled airspace; ATC does not provide separation services to VFR aircraft operating within it.
Below 10,000 feet MSL in Class E, cloud clearance is 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above, and 2,000 feet horizontal, with 3 statute miles visibility.

Special VFR requires flight visibility of at least 1 statute mile, that the aircraft remain clear of clouds, and an ATC clearance; at night it also requires an instrument-rated pilot and an instrument-equipped aircraft.
TFRs are issued under 14 CFR 91.137 through 91.145 to restrict flight in a defined area, often for security, disaster relief, space operations, or VIP movement.
MOAs are not restricted airspace; VFR flight is permitted, but pilots should check for activity and exercise caution due to military training operations.
Prohibited areas are established for security or other reasons, and flight is not allowed within them without specific authorization.

Restricted areas contain unusual, often invisible, hazards such as artillery firing; VFR flight may require clearance from the controlling agency when the area is active, as shown by its activity times on the chart or in NOTAMs.
A warning area extends from 3 nautical miles outward from the U.S. coast, over domestic or international waters or both, and contains activity that may be hazardous to nonparticipating aircraft.
Alert areas inform pilots of areas with a high volume of pilot training or an unusual type of aerial activity; all operations follow normal regulations, but pilots should be especially alert.

MTRs are developed for military flight training, often at speeds in excess of 250 knots and at low altitude; VFR pilots should be especially alert when crossing these routes, depicted on sectional charts.
Victor airways are typically 8 nautical miles wide, 4 nautical miles each side of centerline, extending from 1,200 feet AGL up to but not including 18,000 feet MSL, the floor of Class A airspace.
14 CFR 91.215 generally requires an operating Mode C transponder within 30 nautical miles of a Class B primary airport, from the surface up to 10,000 feet MSL, known as the Mode C veil.
Class B airspace is depicted with solid blue lines, often as concentric rings or irregular shapes, each layer labeled with its floor and ceiling altitudes.

Some Class B airspace areas publish VFR flyways or transition routes that allow VFR traffic to move through or around the area following specific published procedures; pilots should always check current charts and local procedures.
NOTAMs provide timely information about temporary or time-critical conditions, such as runway closures, equipment outages, or new temporary flight restrictions, that could affect a flight's safety.
Classes B, C, and D airspace are established around airports based on traffic volume and complexity, with Class B around the busiest airports and Class D around smaller towered airports.
Airspace adjacent to Class B often sees significant traffic funneling toward the primary airport, so pilots should maintain extra vigilance even when remaining outside the Class B boundaries.
Controlled airspace, Classes A through E, is where ATC provides varying levels of service, from full positive control in Class A to more limited services in Class E; uncontrolled airspace is Class G.
Class D airspace is typically shown with a blue dashed line on sectional charts, representing the lateral boundary of the surface-based controlled airspace around the airport.
A magenta dashed line typically depicts a Class E surface area, where the normally overlying Class E airspace extends all the way down to the ground around that airport.
VFR weather minimums in Class G airspace are generally more restrictive at night than during the day, requiring greater visibility and cloud clearance for safety given reduced visual reference.

At or above 10,000 feet MSL (more than 1,200 feet AGL) in Class E, VFR requires 5 statute miles visibility and cloud clearance of 1,000 feet below, 1,000 feet above, and 1 statute mile horizontally, stricter than the minimums below 10,000 feet.
Weather. Here are the key points. Tap Next any time to skip ahead.
A small temperature-dewpoint spread indicates air is near saturation, favoring fog, haze, or low clouds.
Stable air tends to produce smooth flying conditions, stratus-type clouds, and poor visibility from trapped haze, smoke, or fog.
Unstable air favors vertical development, producing cumulus clouds, turbulence, and typically good visibility away from showers.
Cold fronts often bring a sharp wind shift and falling temperatures behind the front; if the air is moist and unstable, showers or thunderstorms can form along the boundary.
High temperature, high humidity, and high field elevation all raise density altitude, which reduces engine power, lift, and propeller efficiency.

METAR and TAF wind direction is reported in degrees TRUE, so 10008KT means wind from 100 degrees true at 8 knots. Winds given by the tower or on ATIS are in degrees magnetic, matching the runway numbers.
Standard temperature decreases about 2 degrees Celsius (3.5 degrees Fahrenheit) for every 1,000 feet of altitude gained.
TAFs are issued several times a day and forecast conditions at an airport for roughly 24 to 30 hours.
Microbursts produce an intense downdraft that spreads out at the surface, creating a strong headwind followed by a strong tailwind, a severe wind-shear hazard on approach or departure.
A thunderstorm cell develops through the cumulus (building) stage, the mature stage (heaviest rain, strongest drafts), and finally the dissipating stage, dominated by downdrafts.
Radiation fog forms on clear, calm nights when the ground loses heat rapidly by radiation, cooling the adjacent air to its dew point.
Advection fog results from moist air moving horizontally over a colder surface, cooling the air to saturation; it is common along coastlines.
Structural icing requires both visible moisture, such as clouds or precipitation, and a temperature at or below freezing on the parts of the aircraft exposed to the airflow.
Clear ice tends to spread over a surface, forming a smooth, dense, hard layer that can be difficult to see and remove, significantly degrading aerodynamic performance.
Winds and temperatures aloft forecasts show forecast temperatures at various altitudes, letting a pilot estimate where the freezing level, 0 degrees Celsius, will be.
Convective SIGMETs warn of significant convective weather, including severe or embedded thunderstorms, lines of thunderstorms, and hail or tornadoes associated with thunderstorms.
AIRMET Sierra covers IFR conditions, such as ceilings below 1,000 feet or visibility below 3 miles affecting a wide area, and extensive mountain obscuration.
AIRMET Tango covers moderate turbulence, sustained surface winds of 30 knots or more, and low-level wind shear not associated with thunderstorms.
AIRMET Zulu covers moderate icing conditions and forecast freezing levels.
PIREPs report actual weather conditions observed in flight, filling gaps that forecasts alone cannot, and are especially valuable for turbulence, icing, and cloud-top reports.
In the Northern Hemisphere, high-pressure systems have clockwise, outward-flowing winds, while low-pressure systems have counterclockwise, inward-flowing winds.
Virga is visible precipitation trailing from a cloud base that evaporates before reaching the surface; it can be associated with gusty, erratic winds and turbulence underneath.

A temperature inversion is a reversal of the normal temperature-lapse pattern, where temperature increases with height; inversions often trap moisture, smoke, and haze near the surface, reducing visibility.
Strong winds blowing across a mountain ridge can create a wave pattern downwind, producing significant turbulence, strong up and downdrafts, and sometimes distinctive lenticular clouds.
A stationary front occurs when the boundary between two air masses stops advancing, often bringing extended periods of cloudiness and precipitation along its position until it begins moving again.
An occluded front forms when a fast-moving cold front catches up to a slower warm front, lifting the warm air mass off the ground between the two cooler air masses.
Stability indices, such as the lifted index, quantify atmospheric instability, helping forecasters and pilots assess the likelihood and potential severity of thunderstorm development.
Microbursts are strong, localized downdrafts most commonly associated with thunderstorms, though they can also occur with virga from high-based convective clouds.
Ceiling is defined as the height above ground level of the lowest cloud layer reported as broken or overcast, or the vertical visibility into an obscuration, not a clear or scattered layer.
Stable air, particularly beneath a temperature inversion, suppresses vertical mixing, trapping haze, smoke, and other particulates near the surface and reducing visibility.

SIGMETs cover weather hazardous to all categories of aircraft, including severe turbulence, severe icing, widespread dust or sandstorms, and volcanic ash, while AIRMETs address conditions primarily significant to smaller aircraft.
A standard weather briefing covers current conditions, forecasts, relevant NOTAMs, and any applicable advisories such as AIRMETs or SIGMETs along the planned route and altitude.
Aerodynamics. Here are the key points. Tap Next any time to skip ahead.
In straight-and-level, unaccelerated flight, lift equals weight and thrust equals drag; these are the four fundamental forces acting on the airplane.
Angle of attack is the acute angle between the chord line of the airfoil and the relative wind, the direction of airflow relative to the wing.
A stall is caused by exceeding the wing's critical angle of attack; it can occur at any airspeed and any attitude, including at high speed in a steep turn.
Increasing bank angle in a level turn increases load factor, which raises the effective stall speed of the airplane.
In a turn, the aileron that moves down to raise a wing creates more induced drag than the one that moves up, yawing the nose opposite the turn; coordinated rudder input counters this.
P-factor results from the descending propeller blade having a greater angle of attack and producing more thrust than the ascending blade, most pronounced at high power and high angle of attack.
Newton's third law causes the airplane to roll opposite the propeller's rotation; for a standard clockwise-rotating prop, this tends to roll and yaw the airplane to the left.
Flying within about a wingspan of the ground reduces wingtip vortices and induced drag, which can let the airplane fly, or float, at a lower airspeed than it could out of ground effect.
VFE is the maximum speed at which flaps may be extended or used without risking structural damage, marked by the upper end of the white arc on the airspeed indicator.

A more forward CG increases longitudinal stability but requires more up-elevator to flare or raise the nose, and it slightly raises stall speed; an excessively aft CG reduces stability and can make stall recovery difficult.
The ailerons control roll about the longitudinal axis, the elevator controls pitch about the lateral axis, and the rudder controls yaw about the vertical axis.

Modern explanations of lift generally cite both Bernoulli's principle, relating to pressure differences from differing airflow speeds, and Newton's third law, from the wing deflecting air downward; both contribute to the overall lift-generation process.
Induced drag is greatest at low airspeeds and high angles of attack, decreasing as airspeed increases, opposite the trend for parasite drag.

Parasite drag increases with airspeed, roughly with the square of velocity, the opposite trend from induced drag; total drag is the sum of the two and is lowest at the speed for best lift-to-drag ratio.

Wake turbulence is most severe behind aircraft that are heavy, flying slow, and clean (gear and flaps retracted), since a higher angle of attack is needed to produce the required lift, intensifying the vortices.
Staying at or above the preceding larger aircraft's flight path and landing beyond its touchdown point helps a following aircraft avoid the sinking wingtip vortices it leaves behind.
Washout causes the wing root to reach its critical angle of attack, and stall, before the wingtips, helping preserve aileron effectiveness and produce gentler stall characteristics.
Dihedral increases lateral stability: in a sideslip, the lower wing develops a greater angle of attack and more lift, rolling the aircraft back toward wings-level.

A slip occurs when the turn rate is too slow for the bank angle, with the ball displaced to the inside of the turn; a skid occurs when the turn rate is too fast for the bank angle, with the ball displaced to the outside; both are uncoordinated flight.
Load factor increases with bank angle; a 60-degree banked, level turn produces approximately 2 G, which also raises the stall speed by roughly 40 percent.
An accelerated stall happens when the critical angle of attack is exceeded at an airspeed higher than the normal stall speed, typically from increased load factor in a steep turn or abrupt pull-up.

An airplane with spiral instability tends to steepen a bank over time rather than correct it, which can develop into a diving spiral with rapidly increasing airspeed if not corrected, a hazard especially in inadvertent IMC.
Positive static stability describes the initial tendency, after a disturbance, to move back toward the original trimmed condition, a desirable characteristic designed into most training airplanes.
As angle of attack increases, the center of pressure, the point where the resultant aerodynamic force acts, generally moves forward on most conventional airfoils, up to the point of stall.
Lift is proportional to the square of airspeed, among other factors, so doubling airspeed, with angle of attack and other factors unchanged, roughly quadruples the lift produced.
Camber describes the curvature of an airfoil's upper and lower surfaces; a cambered airfoil typically generates more lift at a given angle of attack than a symmetrical one.
Coordinated rudder pressure in the direction of the turn counters the adverse yaw created by differential aileron drag, keeping the turn entry coordinated.
For a given glide configuration, the glide ratio is relatively unaffected by weight, but a heavier airplane must fly faster to achieve that same glide ratio, descending at a higher rate.

A symmetrical airfoil produces no lift at zero angle of attack, since its upper and lower surfaces are mirror images; a cambered airfoil, by contrast, can produce lift even at zero or slightly negative angles of attack.
Aspect ratio is the ratio of wingspan to average chord length; high-aspect-ratio wings, long and narrow, as on gliders, are generally more aerodynamically efficient than low-aspect-ratio wings.

As angle of attack increases toward the critical angle, the boundary layer airflow over the upper wing surface tends to separate from the surface, disrupting smooth lift-producing airflow and leading to a stall.

Trim sets a target airspeed; reducing power without retrimming causes a stable airplane to descend as it seeks to maintain that trimmed airspeed, trading altitude for the energy that power had provided.
Aircraft Systems. Here are the key points. Tap Next any time to skip ahead.

Carb ice can form even in relatively mild, humid conditions, roughly 20 to 70 degrees Fahrenheit, because the venturi effect and fuel vaporization cause significant cooling inside the carburetor throat.
Dual magneto/ignition systems provide redundancy if one system fails and improve combustion efficiency by firing two spark plugs per cylinder.
Fuel injection systems have no carburetor venturi, so they are far less prone to the induction icing associated with float-type carburetors, though some icing can still occur in rare conditions.
The pitot-static system supplies pitot (dynamic) and static pressure to the airspeed indicator, altimeter, and vertical speed indicator.
Traditional attitude and heading indicators are gyroscopic instruments powered by a vacuum/suction system or by electricity, depending on the installation.
Flaps increase the wing's effective camber and area, increasing lift at a given airspeed and adding drag, which allows slower, steeper approaches.
Trim adjusts the force needed on the elevator control to maintain a desired attitude, relieving the pilot from continuously holding pressure.
Engine oil lubricates moving parts, helps dissipate heat, and in many engines also actuates hydraulic components such as a constant-speed propeller governor.

The alternator, or generator, supplies electrical power to the aircraft's systems and recharges the battery while the engine runs; the battery alone powers things when the engine is off or the alternator fails.
Vacuum pump failure affects the vacuum-driven attitude and heading indicators; the pitot-static instruments, and an electric turn coordinator if installed, are typically unaffected.
A constant-speed propeller's governor automatically varies blade pitch to hold the RPM the pilot has selected, improving efficiency across a range of airspeeds and power settings.
A fixed-pitch propeller's blade angle cannot be changed in flight, so it is most efficient at only one airspeed/RPM combination, usually optimized for either climb or cruise performance.
As altitude increases, air density decreases; without leaning, the mixture becomes overly rich because the same fuel flow mixes with less air, so leaning restores the proper fuel-to-air ratio.

Detonation is an abnormal, explosive, uncontrolled burning of the fuel-air charge, which can produce extreme heat and pressure and damage engine components such as pistons; it can result from factors like an overly lean mixture, excessive manifold pressure, or low-octane fuel.
Shock cooling can occur when engine temperature drops too quickly, such as from a rapid power reduction, and is generally avoided by making gradual power changes, particularly during descent.
Static wicks discharge static electric buildup from the airframe into the air smoothly, reducing precipitation static that could otherwise interfere with radio and navigation equipment.

Tricycle gear, with a nosewheel, generally provides better visibility over the nose and more forgiving ground handling than conventional, tailwheel, gear, which is more prone to nose-over and groundloop tendencies, especially in crosswinds.
In many high-wing designs, fuel tanks in the wings sit above the engine, allowing gravity to feed fuel to the carburetor or fuel injection system, often with a pump as a backup.
Cowl flaps regulate airflow through the engine compartment; opening them increases cooling, useful during climb or ground operations, while closing them reduces drag during cruise.
In a wet-wing design, the wing's internal structure is sealed to serve directly as the fuel tank, rather than relying on a separate bladder or rigid tank fitted inside the wing.
An ammeter or loadmeter shows the flow of electrical current in the system, helping a pilot monitor whether the alternator is charging the battery properly or whether the battery is discharging.
Circuit breakers and fuses protect electrical circuits and components from damage by interrupting the circuit if current exceeds a safe level.

During run-up, selecting BOTH is normal operation; briefly switching to L or R individually tests each magneto and should produce a small, expected RPM drop, confirming both ignition systems are functioning; an excessive drop or a dead magneto indicates a problem.

Monitoring oil temperature and pressure helps a pilot catch early signs of engine problems, such as insufficient lubrication, overheating, or a developing mechanical issue, before they become more serious.
The mixture control adjusts the ratio of fuel to air delivered to the engine, allowing the pilot to lean the mixture as altitude increases and air density decreases, maintaining efficient combustion.
Annunciator panels and individual warning lights alert pilots to specific abnormal system conditions, giving an early indication of a developing problem.
The fuel selector valve lets the pilot choose which tank or tanks feed the engine, important for fuel management and maintaining lateral balance.
Performance & W&B. Here are the key points. Tap Next any time to skip ahead.
Higher density altitude reduces engine power output, propeller thrust, and the lift the wing generates, all of which increase the required takeoff roll and reduce climb performance.
The CG must remain within the approved forward and aft limits for the airplane's actual weight, as specified in the POH or AFM.
Useful load equals maximum allowable gross weight minus the aircraft's basic empty weight; it includes pilot, passengers, baggage, and usable fuel.
Basic empty weight includes the standard airframe, powerplant, fixed equipment, unusable fuel, and full operating fluids such as engine oil, but excludes usable fuel and payload.
Because the engine produces less power and the propeller and wings are less efficient in less dense air, both climb rate and climb angle decrease at higher density altitudes.
The standard atmosphere model defines sea-level conditions as 29.92 inHg and 15 degrees Celsius (59 degrees Fahrenheit).
Pressure altitude is read directly from the altimeter when the Kollsman window is set to 29.92 inHg, the standard datum.
A headwind component reduces groundspeed at a given airspeed, which shortens the ground roll and total distance needed to reach liftoff speed.
Short-field technique commonly involves maximum performance power application and using the flap setting and speeds, often VX, best angle of climb, recommended in the POH to clear obstacles.
A heavier airplane needs more lift to remain airborne, which at the same angle of attack requires more airspeed; therefore stall speed increases with weight.
Takeoff, landing, and climb performance charts typically account for pressure altitude, temperature, aircraft weight, and wind component, since all affect performance.

A downhill slope helps acceleration during takeoff, generally shortening the takeoff roll, but works against deceleration during landing, generally lengthening the landing roll; an uphill slope has the opposite effects.
Soft or rough surfaces, such as grass, increase rolling friction and resistance, lengthening the takeoff ground roll compared to a smooth, paved runway.
Maximum gross weight is the heaviest weight at which an aircraft is certificated to operate safely, as specified by the manufacturer and limited in the POH/AFM.
A moment represents the rotational effect a weight has around the reference datum; heavier items farther from the datum contribute a larger moment, shifting the center of gravity more significantly.
Service ceiling is the density altitude at which the maximum rate of climb decreases to 100 feet per minute; absolute ceiling, by contrast, is the altitude at which climb rate reaches zero.

True airspeed is calibrated airspeed corrected for non-standard pressure and temperature; as altitude increases and air density decreases, true airspeed becomes progressively greater than indicated or calibrated airspeed for a given dynamic pressure.
VY, best rate of climb, gains the greatest altitude per unit of time; VX, best angle of climb, instead gains the greatest altitude per unit of horizontal distance, useful for clearing obstacles.
VX is typically a slower speed than VY, chosen specifically to gain the most altitude over the shortest horizontal distance, important when climbing out over obstacles.
Interpolation involves estimating a value that falls between two charted data points by proportionally adjusting between them, rather than simply rounding to the nearest listed value.

Climb performance depends significantly on flying at the correct climb speed recommended in the POH for the given conditions; deviating from it, especially flying too slow or too fast, reduces climb performance.
Rate of climb describes the vertical speed at which an aircraft gains altitude, typically expressed in feet per minute.

Useful load includes usable fuel along with the weight of occupants, baggage, and cargo, while payload more narrowly refers to the revenue-producing weight such as passengers and cargo, excluding fuel.
An aft CG reduces longitudinal stability, can make the airplane more prone to pitch oscillations, and can make stall recovery more difficult since there is less nose-down pitching tendency available.

Published performance figures are typically achieved by a new aircraft in top mechanical condition, flown by a skilled test pilot under precise technique; actual performance by an average pilot in a used aircraft is often somewhat less favorable, so prudent pilots add a safety margin.

Using actual, current conditions, such as the reported wind, temperature, and pressure, rather than optimistic assumptions, gives a more realistic and safer performance estimate for the flight being planned.

Because published performance is often achieved under near-ideal test conditions, prudent pilots commonly add a safety margin to planned takeoff and landing distances rather than planning to the exact published minimums.
Navigation. Here are the key points. Tap Next any time to skip ahead.
Sectional charts use a scale of 1:500,000, roughly 6.86 nautical miles per inch.
A VOR radial is a magnetic course measured outward FROM the station; there are 360 radials, one for each degree.
TO/FROM simply tells the pilot whether flying the selected course would lead toward or away from the station; it does not indicate heading or track directly.
Variation is the angular difference between true north and magnetic north, which changes with location; deviation, by contrast, is compass error caused by the aircraft's own magnetic influences.

True course, corrected for wind, gives true heading; adding or subtracting variation gives magnetic heading; correcting that for deviation, from the compass correction card, gives the compass heading to fly.
Pilotage means navigating by visually matching ground features to a chart, as opposed to dead reckoning, which relies on computed heading, time, speed, and wind.
WAAS augments GPS signals to improve accuracy and provide integrity monitoring, enabling GPS approaches with vertical guidance, such as LPV approaches.
Alternating white and green flashes mark a lighted civilian land airport; other combinations (such as white-yellow for water airports) identify other facility types.
Using a single time reference, UTC (Zulu), avoids confusion that would arise from pilots and controllers in different local time zones communicating about schedules and times.
The wind correction angle is added to or subtracted from the course to determine the heading the pilot must fly to track the intended course over the ground despite wind drift.
Blue airport symbols on a sectional chart denote airports with an operating control tower; magenta denotes non-towered airports.
Sectional charts typically show an obstruction's height above mean sea level as the bold number, with its height above ground level shown in smaller type, often in parentheses.
FAA guidance generally allows a tolerance of plus or minus 4 degrees for a VOT or ground checkpoint check.
DME measures the slant-range distance between the aircraft and a ground station, typically also displaying groundspeed and time to station.
The ADF needle points to the relative bearing of the tuned NDB station; combined with the aircraft's heading, the pilot can determine magnetic bearing to or from the station.
RAIM uses redundant satellite information to verify the integrity of the GPS position solution, alerting the pilot if the signal quality cannot be relied upon for navigation.
Effective checkpoints for pilotage should be prominent, unique landmarks easily recognized from altitude and not easily confused with similar nearby features.
A VFR flight plan, when not closed within a reasonable time after the estimated arrival, prompts Flight Service to initiate search-and-rescue procedures, a key safety benefit of filing one.
The CDI needle deflects left or right to show the aircraft's position relative to the selected VOR course or radial, not the aircraft's heading directly.
Isogonic lines connect points having the same amount of magnetic variation; the agonic line specifically connects points of zero variation, where true north and magnetic north coincide.
